Content:
Can we apply Euler's method to approximate solutions to second-order initial value problems, such as the one below?

Content:
[MATH: xy'' - y' - y = 2x, \qquad y(1) = -1, \quad y'(1) = 1]

Content:
Well, for a second-order initial value problem,

Content:
[MATH: y'' = f(x, y, y'), \qquad y(a) = c, \quad y'(a) = d,]

Content:
we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

Content:
[MATH: {y^{′} = z,|y(a) = c,; z^{′} = f(x, y, z),|z(a) = d,]

Content:
before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation:

Content:
[MATH: {Δy = y^{′} ⋅ Δx; Δz = z^{′} ⋅ Δx]

Content:
The new values are then given by [MATH: y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y] and [MATH: z_\text{new} = z + \Delta z.]

Content:
In the example above, we set up Euler's method by first isolating [MATH: y''] so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable [MATH: z{:}]

Content:
[MATH: xy^{″} − y^{′} − y|= 2x; xy^{″}|= y + y^{′} + 2x; y^{″}|= (y + y^{′})/(x) + 2]

Content:
Then, we substitute our new variable [MATH: z=y',] [MATH: z'=y''] in the above. This gives the system

Content:
[MATH: {y^{′} = z,|y(1) = − 1; z^{′} = (y + z)/(x) + 2,|z(1) = 1.]

Content:
On the next slide, we will approximate values for this system using step size [MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac12.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Can we apply Euler's method to approximate solutions to second-order initial value problems, such as the one below?

Content:
[MATH: xy'' - y' - y = 2x, \qquad y(1) = -1, \quad y'(1) = 1]

Content:
Well, for a second-order initial value problem,

Content:
[MATH: y'' = f(x, y, y'), \qquad y(a) = c, \quad y'(a) = d,]

Content:
we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

Content:
[MATH: {y^{′} = z,|y(a) = c,; z^{′} = f(x, y, z),|z(a) = d,]

Content:
before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation:

Content:
[MATH: {Δy = y^{′} ⋅ Δx; Δz = z^{′} ⋅ Δx]

Content:
The new values are then given by [MATH: y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y] and [MATH: z_\text{new} = z + \Delta z.]

Content:
In the example above, we set up Euler's method by first isolating [MATH: y''] so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable [MATH: z{:}]

Content:
[MATH: xy^{″} − y^{′} − y|= 2x; xy^{″}|= y + y^{′} + 2x; y^{″}|= (y + y^{′})/(x) + 2]

Content:
Then, we substitute our new variable [MATH: z=y',] [MATH: z'=y''] in the above. This gives the system

Content:
[MATH: {y^{′} = z,|y(1) = − 1; z^{′} = (y + z)/(x) + 2,|z(1) = 1.]

Content:
On the next slide, we will approximate values for this system using step size [MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac12.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
We now apply the update rules [MATH: \Delta y = y' \cdot \Delta x] and [MATH: \Delta z = z' \cdot \Delta x] to our system below starting at [MATH: x=1] with step size [MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac12.]

Content:
[MATH: {y^{′} = z,|y(1) = − 1; z^{′} = (y + z)/(x) + 2,|z(1) = 1.]

Content:
We'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data [MATH: y(1)=-1] and [MATH: z(1)=1.]

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: y] | [MATH: y'] | [MATH: \Delta y] | [MATH: z] | [MATH: z'] | [MATH: \Delta z] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: -1] | | | [MATH: 1] | | |

Content:
We compute [MATH: y'] and [MATH: \Delta y,] [MATH: z'] and [MATH: \Delta z] (using the values of [MATH: x], [MATH: y,] and [MATH: z,] in the first row), and the values of [MATH: x_\text{new},] [MATH: y_\text{new},] and [MATH: z_\text{new}] using Euler's method:

Content:
[MATH: y^{′}|= z = 1; z^{′}|= (y + z)/(x) + 2 = (− 1 + 1)/(1) + 2 = 2; Δy|= y^{′} ⋅ Δx = 1 ⋅ (1)/(2) = (1)/(2); Δz|= z^{′} ⋅ Δx = 2 ⋅ (1)/(2) = 1; x_{new}|= x + Δx = 1 + (1)/(2) = (3)/(2); y_{new}|= y + Δy = − 1 + (1)/(2) = − (1)/(2); z_{new}|= z + Δz = 1 + 1 = 2]

Content:
We add these values to our table.

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: y] | [MATH: y'] | [MATH: \Delta y] | [MATH: z] | [MATH: z'] | [MATH: \Delta z] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \dfrac12] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \dfrac32] | [MATH: -\dfrac12] | | | [MATH: 2] | | |

Content:
After several steps, we obtain the following table of values.

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: y] | [MATH: y'] | [MATH: \Delta y] | [MATH: z] | [MATH: z'] | [MATH: \Delta z] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \dfrac12] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \dfrac32] | [MATH: -\dfrac12] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: \dfrac32] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: \dfrac12] | [MATH: \dfrac72] | [MATH: \dfrac74] | [MATH: \dfrac72] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 2] |
| [MATH: \dfrac52] | [MATH: \dfrac94] | | | [MATH: \dfrac{11}2] | | |

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: y\left(\dfrac52\right) \approx \dfrac94] and [MATH: y'\left(\dfrac52\right) = z\left(\dfrac52\right) \approx \dfrac{11}2.]

Content:
Notice that this approach of splitting a second-order ODE into a system of first-order ODEs is not specific to Euler's method. Indeed, we could apply any numerical method component-wise to approximate the solution to a second-order ODE once split into a system of first-order ODEs!
